name: Walliser German of Visperterminen, Upper Valais
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

catalog_quote: § 24. Spezielles über die Wortbetonung. 1. Einfache Wörter: a) In nichtzusammengesetzten deutschen Wörtern trägt immer die Wurzelsilbe den Starkton. Der stärkste Nebenton liegt in drei- und mehrsilbigen Wörtern meistens auf der letzten Silbe: Tǣ́rbinèr Visperterminer; fíɒrlinù die Finger rasch bewegen, zB. beim Klavierspielen; — nur wenn die zweitletzte Silbe einen langen Vokal oder schwere Konsonanz enthält, wird sie betont: ámeìsa Ameise; fịšterlòxti finstere. b) In Fremdwörtern wird der Starkton zum Teil ebenfalls auf die erste Silbe zurückgezogen: áde und ádji adieu; ále allez!; álo allons!; altár Altar als Simplex hat gewöhnlich die fremde Betonung auf der letzten Silbe, dagegen áltardiəner Altardiener; ... [p. 20] Ebenso viele Lehnwörter, meist jüngere, belassen den Ton auf einer spätern, bezw. auf der letzten Silbe, zB. adrǣ́ss m. Adresse; altár s. oben; ammalétta Omelette; ... 2. In nominalen Zusammensetzungen ist, wie anderswo, der erste Bestandteil in den meisten Fällen Träger des Starktons ... [p. 21] 3. Auf dem zweiten Gliede liegt der Ton bei manchen Zusammensetzungen von Adj. + Subst.; es sind dies vor allem Lokal- und Flurnamen

new_statements.quote: a) In nichtzusammengesetzten deutschen Wörtern trägt immer die Wurzelsilbe den Starkton. Der stärkste Nebenton liegt in drei- und mehrsilbigen Wörtern meistens auf der letzten Silbe: Tǟrbiner Visperterminer; fịrlinu die Finger rasch bewegen, zB. beim Klavierspielen; — nur wenn die zweitletzte Silbe einen langen Vokal oder schwere Konsonanz enthält, wird sie betont: ámeisa Ameise; fịšterlöxti finstere.
new_statements.translation: a) In non-compound German words the root syllable always carries the main stress. In words of three or more syllables the strongest secondary stress mostly lies on the last syllable: Tǟrbiner 'person from Visperterminen'; fịrlinu 'to move the fingers quickly, e.g. when playing the piano'; — only when the penultimate syllable contains a long vowel or heavy consonance is it (the penult) stressed: ámeisa 'ant'; fịšterlöxti 'dark ones'.
new_statements.citation: Wipf, Elisa. 1908. Die Mundart von Visperterminen im Wallis. Inaugural-Dissertation Universität Zürich. Frauenfeld: Huber & Co.

Der stärkste Nebenton liegt in drei- und mehrsilbigen Wörtern meistens auf der letzten Silbe.. — nur wenn die zweitletzte Silbe einen langen Vokal oder schwere Konsonanz enthält, wird sie betont.. Ameise.. finstere." The only differences are in the transcribed diale…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress is fixed on the root (stem) syllable of native words, which in Alemannic is normally the first syllable of the stem; prefixes (e.g. bitsíe 'to obtain', gitséigt 'shown', antwég 'in the way' in § 23) are unstressed. Loanwords frequently keep their foreign late or final stress (altár, adréss, famíli, orgalíst), though some are retracted to the initial syllable (ádje, fámos). Nominal compounds stress the first member; place names and some Adj+N compounds (hōbǖl 'Hochbühl', rothórn) stress the second.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Strongest secondary stress usually on the final syllable of 3+-syllable words, shifted to the penult when the penult has a long vowel or heavy consonant cluster (§ 24.1a, p. 19). § 23 (pp. 18–19) stresses that the dynamic gap between stressed and unstressed syllables is far smaller than in Standard German or any other Swiss German dialect (only 3–4 strength grades audible), which the author links to the preservation of full final vowels.
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords with retained foreign final/late stress (list pp. 19–20, incl. truncations melikxáner 'Amerikaner', strumént 'Instrument'); compound adjectives spoken with roughly equal stress on both members; place-name compounds and a few Adj+N compounds stressed on the second member; some items with vacillating stress (alwärd 'albern', p. 30 note; jedwedre 'each' with initial or second-member stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (isolated words and compounds); the author separately describes a strong musical (pitch) accent at word and sentence level (§ 25–28, pp. 21–23), calling the dialect a 'singing' one in which phrasing is carried more by pitch than by dynamic stress. Description of the Visperterminen village dialect, Upper Valais (Oberwallis), Switzerland.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes the village dialect of Visperterminen, Upper Valais (Oberwallis), Switzerland — i.e. the Walliser German 'Heimattal' variety rather than one of the Walser emigrant colonies. Glottolog 5.1 files Wipf 1908 under wals1238 (Walser, ISO wae, alt. name 'Walser German'), which covers Valais Highest Alemannic together with the Walser settlements in Graubünden, Vorarlberg, Liechtenstein, Piedmont, Aosta and Ticino; no separate Glottolog dialect code is listed for Visperterminen. The second opened source (Russ 2004) is for Bosco Gurin, a Ticino Walser colony, and is consistent (first vowel of disyllables stressed) but gives no explicit rule.

new_statements.quote: p. 15: "Der Akzent wird nur bezeichnet, wenn er von der hd. Betonungsweise abweicht." — § 25, p. 27-28: "1. Der exspiratorische Wortakzent. a) Im einfachen Wort sind die Stärkeabstufungen zwischen betonten und schwach- (bezw. un-) betonten Silben weniger ausgeprägt als zB. im Schweizer Mittelland, immerhin aber doch noch deutlich und in keiner Weise etwa mit dem Französischen zu vergleichen ... b) Im zusammengesetzten Wort: α) In der Mehrzahl der Fälle gilt Anfangsbetonung ... c. Betonung fremder Wörter. α) Alte Lehnwörter haben den Starkton allgemein auf die erste Silbe zurückgezogen ... β) Die fremde Betonung beibehalten haben: die Feminina auf -i (mhd. -îe) und -ō wie pərtíi Partei; pərső Person ..."
new_statements.translation: p. 15: 'The accent is marked only where it deviates from the High German manner of stressing.' § 25: '1. The expiratory word accent. a) In the simple word the gradations of force between stressed and weakly stressed (or unstressed) syllables are less pronounced than e.g. in the Swiss Mittelland, but still distinct and in no way comparable to French ... b) In the compound word: α) in the majority of cases initial stress holds ... c. Stress of foreign words. α) Old loanwords have generally retracted the main stress onto the first syllable ... β) Foreign stress has been kept by the feminines in -i (MHG -îe) and -ō, e.g. pərtíi "Partei", pərső "Person" ...'

new_statements.relation_note: Same stress type as the existing Wipf 1908 statement for Visperterminen (root/initial main stress in native simplex words, compounds initial, loans partly with foreign stress, 'singing' pitch contour) — but the work describes the Walser colony dialect of Obersaxen (Graubünden), not Visperterminen; both are filed under wals1238 (Glottolog attaches Brun 1918 to wals1238). Brun states the root-stress default only indirectly (accent unmarked = High German stress), hence medium confidence.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress follows the High German pattern (main stress on the root/first syllable of native simplex words), so Brun marks accent only where a form deviates from it; the stressed/unstressed contrast is weaker than in Swiss Plateau dialects but still clear. Compounds are mostly initial-stressed, with a set of second-member-stressed compounds (card names by contrast stress; miták 'Mittag', nüu(w)jár 'Neujahr', færtəlštúnt, genitive+noun compounds and many field names keeping old phrasal stress). Old loans retract stress to the first syllable (xetti, xappala 'Kapelle', samət); later loans keep foreign (late) stress (pərtíi, səldát, tabákx, verbs in -íæræ); given names now mostly initial-stressed (jōsep, færdınant) with exceptions (aləksándər). § 25.2: a markedly 'singing' dialect in which high pitch and dynamic stress often do not coincide, weak syllables frequently being higher-pitched than stressed ones.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No general secondary-stress rule stated; derivational suffixes -læxt, -haft, -šaft and -sam are described as carrying Nebenton and therefore escaping vowel reduction (§ 97.11, § 96 Anm. 5, printed pp. ~95-97); § 25.b.γ notes compounds with roughly level stress on both members (pflætšnass, xələšwärts).
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds with stress on the second member (card names, Mittag/Neujahr/Viertelstunde type, genitive compounds, place and field names such as obərsaksa with retracted stress vs. grösstóbal etc. with preserved late stress); loans in -i/-ō and recent loans with foreign stress; some given names (aləksándər, margretæ, batíštæ) keeping non-initial stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Brun 1918 describes the Walser German of Obersaxen (Surselva, Canton Graubünden), a Walser colony dialect filed under the same glottocode wals1238 but a different locality from the catalog record's Visperterminen (Upper Valais); Brun himself notes features 'vom Wallis mitgebracht'. Bohnenberger 1913 (not opened) covers the Valais Heimattal and the outer Walser settlements.
